HEADLINE: End of Barty party leaves Open exposed
TEXT:
Australian Open organisers face a final series devoid of a marquee match-up, and without fan favourite Ash Barty after her shock exit yesterday, following Rafael Nadal and Serena Williams out the door.

Last night's knockout match between Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer leaves just one household name in this weekend's finals.

Some are billing tonight's semi-final clash between young guns German Alexander Zverev and Austrian Dominic Thiem as a changing of the guard.

"When you have the crowd favourites it's always helpful for the broadcast audience and people watching around the world," Tennis Australia CEO Craig Tiley told The Australian Financial Review when the tournament kicked off.

The low-profile finals are the latest in a long list of challenges that Tennis Australia has faced this year, including smoke from the bushfires, heat, rain, climate protesters and transport strikes.

There are also renewed calls to change the name of Margaret Court Arena, after a fiery interview with tennis great John McEnroe yesterday to explain his on-court protest of earlier in the week reignited the controversy.

But Tennis Australia chairman Jayne Hrdlicka - the former CEO of A2 Milk - said it was not responsible for the naming of stadiums. Tennis Australia is a tenant of the Melbourne Olympic Park Trust, which is overseen by a board appointed by the Victorian government and chaired by former Shell executive and Orica chairman Russell Caplan.

McEnroe and Martina Navratilova sparked global headlines after Navratilova climbed into the umpire's chair to address the crowd at the end of her Legends doubles match on Tuesday, before the television feed was cut off as she was speaking. McEnroe then joined Navratilova on court carrying a banner reading "Evonne Goolagong Arena".

They later apologised for breaking protocol.

But in a fiery interview yesterday, McEnroe doubled down on his views before hanging up the phone.

"It could have been done better and more effectively. But in terms of regret doing it, no," he said on 3AW in Melbourne.

"I loved Evonne Goolagong when I was a kid and I think she represents to me everything positive about what you'd want a stadium to be named."

Grilled on what in particular Margaret Court, now a Pentecostal pastor in Western Australia, had said to upset him, McEnroe pointed to her claims that LGBTQ teaching in schools was controlled by the devil.

"Her comments about race in the past, homophopia for starters, her comments these people are connected to the devil are the comments I feel go over the line for people who are already marginalised," McEnroe said.

"It's up to them to decide whether or not they think it's appropriate - with all the comments she has made ... that despite her tennis achievements, which are obviously numerous, she would continue to have her name on the arena," before McEnroe told host Neil Mitchell he had to go and hung up.

In a letter after her protest, Navratilova described Evonne Goolagong as the "embodiment of what a role model or hero truly is".

HEADLINE: Fresh ACOSS call to raise Newstart
TEXT:
The nation's peak welfare body has urged Treasurer Josh Frydenberg to spur the national economy with $16 billion in new spending, stimulus which it says will boost wages and employment.

The Australian Council of Social Service says reviving wages and jobs growth while guaranteeing government services and unemployment benefits should be the May budget's top priorities, along with responding to extreme weather events and the changing climate.

In a submission to the pre-budget process, ACOSS called for spending on new social housing, support for drought-affected communities and better aged care and mental health services, at a net cost of $4.5 billion.

The plan would preserve a $5.8 billion budget surplus.

Central to the proposal is a $3.8 billion increase to the Newstart unemployment payment, which chief executive Cassandra Goldie said must rise by $95 a week.

Welfare groups had campaigned for a $75 a week increase, but Dr Goldie said rising cost-of-living meant that amount would now be inadequate for vulnerable job seekers.

She warned government service failures and stagnant wage growth could not become a "new normal" in Australia.

"Our budget submission makes the case for a well-targeted fiscal stimulus package including an immediate boost to Newstart, investment in social housing construction and energy efficiency," she said.

"Tax cuts and investment incentives are much less effective in boosting the economy per dollar spent and do little to assist those on the lowest incomes."

The Morrison government has resisted calls from welfare groups, the Business Council of Australia, trade unions and former prime minister John Howard to increase the rate of Newstart.

Newstart, which is updated twice a year in line with inflation, has been stagnant in real terms since 1994.

Mr Frydenberg's planned $5 billion surplus is already under pressure from the cost of summer bushfires. Last week he couldn't say if a surplus remained likely, given the unknown economic impact of the crisis.

ACOSS said calls for fiscal action by the Reserve Bank, International Monetary Fund and the OECD should prompt action from the Coalition, describing stimulus spending as more effective than the bringing forward of planned personal income tax cuts.

Its costings are based on an $11.5 billion increase in government revenues, including through abolition of the $6.3 billion private health insurance rebate and the $500 million extended Medicare safety net.

ACOSS said its proposals, including $2.3 billion for in-home aged care packages, would increase the impact of budget savings across the forward estimates and help offset rising costs of health, aged care and the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

Business groups and economists last week warned the government would need to halve the size of its planned surpluses in the next 18 months and pump $5 billion into a business investment allowance to lift the economy.

ACOSS also called for a boost to rent assistance worth about $20 a week, costing the budget about $1.2 billion a year.

Mr Frydenberg will hand down the budget on May 12.

HEADLINE: Banks warn against hasty probe response
TEXT:
The banking industry lobby wants Treasury to ensure consultation on Hayne legislation is thorough and robust to avoid "knee-jerk" responses that could create a "ripple effect across the entire economy".

With about 25 per cent of federal Parliament's legislative agenda this year involving royal commission recommendations, Australian Banking Association chief executive Anna Bligh said "if you screw too tightly on some of the regulations, you can have inadvertent impacts".

Banks did not oppose any specific recommendations, she said, but were "determined to have the robust discussion that is required to get it right, because if we get it wrong, there is a lot at stake".

Of commissioner Kenneth Hayne's 76 recommendations, 54 were directed at the government, which has committed to responding to 26 in legislation to be consulted on and introduced by June 30, with a further seven by December 31.

Issues to be codified this year included an end to hawking of insurance products, creating a statutory duty for APRA and ASIC to cooperate and a new body to oversee them, and extending an executive accountability regime to all financial services players.

Royal commissions would inevitably "find some holes in the legislative and regulatory landscape", Ms Bligh said.

"As you go about plugging those holes, it is important to do it in a way that is thoughtful and not knee-jerk.

"What we are dealing with here has a ripple effect across the entire economy, and across the lives and financial wellbeing of every Australian."

Banking leaders agreed on the importance of ensuring a proper balance was struck to ensure banks remained willing to support the economy.

"It is about making sure we have the right balance in terms of how the government and regulators act and how we act, to ensure number one we are protecting, but also to ensure we are providing the engine in terms of economic growth," Bank of Queensland chief executive George Frazis told a Trans-Tasman Business Circle event yesterday, ahead of the first anniversary next week of the Hayne report being delivered.

"This is a complex system," Mr Frazis said. "You really have to take time to make sure that it makes sense, it is easy to understand, that there is no ambiguity and there are no unintended consequences."

The discussion revealed banks were still grappling with how to reform culture in response to the inquiry's critique of their excessive focus on profit, but the industry understood the community had increased expectations.

With swathes of the country recovering from devastating bushfires, Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn said the financial services industry "stands united to assist the rebuilding of those communities".

Pointing to changes to the banking code of conduct increasing protections, including for small businesses, Mr Comyn, who is chairman of the ABA, said: "You have to give people a reasonable period to respond. Something completely outside their control is quite different to a set of deteriorating business conditions."

He pushed back at suggestions Hayne, or ASIC's "Wagyu and shiraz" case against Westpac, had forced banks to tighten up lending.

"We, and I am sure many others, have not changed a single thing in response to the [ASIC/Westpac] legal case," he said, noting that rising unemployment was the biggest risk for banks.

Liberal MP Jason Falinski asked from the audience whether panel members were concerned the report had degraded the profit motive of business. Mr Frazis responded that adopting longer-term thinking would help banks balance the interests of competing stakeholders.

"The minute an organisation starts to take a short-term view, you start making bad trade-offs amongst all the stakeholders," Mr Frazis said. "Good customer outcomes over the long term are good for our shareholders, our communities, regulators and government - it all aligns."

Fiona Guthrie, chief executive of Financial Counselling Australia, said: "We need very profitable and strong banks, but profit at any cost is a problem."

Hayne had made it clear that "it is profit within what is good for the community, not profit for its own sake", she said.

HEADLINE: Amid small hints of resentment, banned adviser sees silver lining
TEXT:
Financial advice A high-profile Hayne casualty speaks out.

Nearly two years since his spectacular fall from grace during the banking royal commission, former financial adviser Sam Henderson says the inquiry was a "gift".

"I thought I'd built a life of perfection, so to get dragged down from that and have a slap in the face there is a healthiness to that to some extent," Henderson tells The Australian Financial Review over morning coffee on Sydney's northern beaches.

"It creates an opportunity - it is what I call the gift of the royal commission - had I not gone through that, I might not be as empathetic or active as I am now."

Few financial advisers have enjoyed his success or public profile. He carved out a rare career as an American-style money guru, fielding questions from amateur traders on TV, penning a regular column for The Australian Financial Review, and hosting industry conferences. And that was in his spare time. He was also chief executive of Henderson Maxwell, an advice and accounting firm held up as a blueprint for others to emulate: self-licensed, independent of the big banks, a pioneer of the now ubiquitous managed discretionary account model.

But a high-flying career that took decades to build, unravelled in just hours when Henderson came under intense cross-examination by Rowena Orr, QC, as the Hayne royal commission made a brief detour to the independent financial advice sector in April 2018.

That afternoon's proceedings, which saw Henderson accused of providing "risible" advice to former client and Fair Work Commissioner, Donna McKenna, ultimately contributed to a three-year ban from the corporate regulator.

Having found solace in the musings of Texan motivational speaker and professor Brene Brown - who talks about "sharing the shame" - Henderson is taking his message to financial advisers and other small business owners one-on-one as a business coach.

He tells his clients that the personal image they have built up around themselves is "just a narrative" and one that can be changed, adding a compelling reminder of the meaning of life.

"All I need in life is my kids and my surfboard," he says. "And if I have those two things I know I am going to have pretty strong mental health."

Though he worries he has lost his public platform, he says he is still an advocate for financial advice and advisers, encouraged by messages from former clients and competitors.

"The problem is that the industry is feeling the impact but doesn't talk about this stuff, it is shrouded in shame," he says.

"And many deal with it by adopting the opposite position and a sense of arrogance about them. They're the ones that are probably most susceptible to being shot down in the future."

As the conversation delves deeper, some signs of resentment towards the royal commission also start to emerge.

He says there was an "imbalance" between his crime and the punishment - a thesis at odds with ASIC and the royal commission, which heard his firm had funnelled clients into in-house products, exaggerated his education credentials and even impersonated Ms McKenna on a phone call to her super fund.

But he stops short of adopting the victim label.

"I don't think we [witnesses] are victims, that's not productive, we are all part of the same system," he says.

"But I do feel for the consumers. They want a personal, simplistic approach to advice and they're not getting it. And it's only getting worse."

HEADLINE: For Luca, it's more talk, less activism
TEXT:
To Luca Belgiorno-Nettis, the biggest problem facing humanity isn't climate change: it's fixing the adversarial and unproductive nature of politics. "The real challenge is building consensus [in public decision making]," says Belgiorno-Nettis, who knows more than most about conflict, having been forced out of chairmanship of the Biennale of Sydney in 2014.

Constructive dialogue was what was missing from the events of 2014, he says, in his first full interview on his dramatic ousting from the arts fair that his father founded 41 years earlier and into which his family had poured millions of dollars. His resignation followed an artist boycott of the Biennale because of the Belgiorno-Nettis' family's links to Transfield Services, which operated detention centres on Manus Island and Nauru.

And he feels that constructive dialogue has been increasingly absent from the public realm since. "The recent bushfires highlight the point," he says. "Our political leaders are spending so much time and energy point-scoring that people get turned off. It's not the fault of the politicians; it's the system that incentivises them to be belligerent."

Since leaving the Biennale, Belgiorno-Nettis has focused his philanthropic time and money on newDemocracy, an organisation he had founded in 2007 to promote "deliberative democracy", based on the ancient Greek model of representation by civic lottery, in which he has since invested $4 million. After some frustratingly slow years, Belgiorno-Nettis thinks the concept's time has come, as evidenced by moves to institutionalise citizen juries in Belgium and the success of the Irish citizens' assemblies that were in the historic referendums legalising abortion and same-sex marriage.

As for 2014: "It was terrible because I'd been there for 13 years as chairman, my father started it and my [younger brother Guido] had taken over and resuscitated it," Belgiorno-Nettis says, the first time he's talked about the Biennale events at any length. "For it to finish like that was so sad. We were highly invested in it emotionally. The whole concept and mission and team we had built were something we believed in absolutely. And we thought it was on a roll, going from strength to strength."

Six years on, there doesn't appear to have been any winners from 2014, beyond activism itself, which - inspired partly by the Biennale boycott - has flowered internationally, from the campaign to oust BP as a major sponsor of the Tate in London, to picketing at New York's Museum of Modern Art because one of its directors, BlackRock CEO Lawrence Fink, had invested in private prisons. On the eve of the 22nd Biennale, which opens on March 14, Managing Director Barbara Moore says the organisation was "traumatised" by the events of 2014, since which staff have turned over twice and the board and MD position three times.

Audience numbers in 2014 and 2016 were below the 665,000 who attended the controversy-free Biennale of 2012 but recovered to 855,000 in 2018. The Biennale is hoping one million people will attend this year's 98-artist extravaganza, curated by indigenous artist Brook Andrew.

More broadly, the controversy was seen as the catalyst to the significant cuts to Federal government arts funding in its wake. Meanwhile, the Spanish company Ferrovial that took over Transfield - rebadged as Broadspectrum after the controversy - in 2016 didn't tender the following year for the Manus and Nauru contracts, which the federal government awarded to Paladin. Hence the biggest losers from 2014 may yet prove to be refugees themselves and the Australian taxpayers, who have since shelled out more than half a billion.

Brook Turner's feature on Luca Belgiorno-Nettis appears on www.afr.com and inside the Arts & Culture issue of The Australian Financial Review Magazine, inside today's Financial Review.

HEADLINE: Regulators may have shielded JPMorgan: ANZ
TEXT:
ANZ has questioned whether corporate and competition watchdogs engaged in collusion and abuses of power and process in their investigations of allegedly criminal conduct by Deutsche Bank, Citigroup and JPMorgan over a failed capital raising in 2015.

JPMorgan is the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's star witness in a landmark cartel case against the other three banks.

ANZ suggested the competition regulator may have pushed the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) not to pursue JPMorgan in an investigation into a $2.5 billion capital raising from ANZ shares as it did not want the bank's reputation to appear sullied in court on Thursday.

A shortfall arose during the raising and Citi, Deutsche and JPMorgan, which were underwriting the placement, later took up the excess shares to sell - events scrutinised by both regulators.

The ACCC alleged the decision to withhold the shares from the market constituted cartel conduct, leading to unprecedented criminal charges against ANZ, Citi, Deutsche and six of their executives by the federal prosecutor.

JPMorgan received an immunity marker - protection from prosecution that is only offered to one member of alleged cartels - in exchange for its co-operation with the case.

Tim Game, SC, appearing for ANZ, suggested this meant the ACCC had a vested interest in the bank appearing reputable in its conduct during the capital raising and the court might need to consider whether the ACCC put pressure on ASIC not to pursue JPMorgan.

"It would ... be an abuse of power if ASIC had decided not to bring proceedings against JPMorgan for the reason that the ACCC had successfully put pressure on them," he said.

The intervention might have been "not just for JPMorgan's benefit but also for their own benefit, because they did not want their immunity applicant sullied by [accusations] of insider trading".

ANZ raised the possibility of abuse of power and collusion when arguing against an attempt by ASIC to claim privilege over documents the bank subpoenaed.

Mr Game alleged that the "pressure" might have occurred from September 2017, which was "quite a long way into ASIC's investigation".

He claimed JPMorgan, through its lawyers from Gilbert+Tobin, approached the ACCC not in respect of the ACCC investigation, but that of ASIC.

An ACCC officer then allegedly contacted a senior officer at ASIC and, "after some to-ing and fro-ing", reached an understanding of what each regulator would investigate.

ASIC slammed the "very serious" allegations, including that of abuse of process, as "outrageous".

Appearing for ASIC, Sue McNicol, QC, said ANZ had only given the regulator its submissions on Tuesday, even though the hearing began two days later.

The barrister proposed ASIC provide a closed affidavit that would directly respond to the allegations to the court, but refused to hand over the full lists of documents requested by the banks on grounds of legal privilege.

But magistrate Jennifer Giles denied the suggestion.

Mr Game instead pushed for ASIC to hand over the full documents the defence had requested.

The regulator has claimed various protections to withhold certain parts of the evidence, including legal professional privilege and public interest immunity, and has argued that sharing information about its processes could compromise future investigations and stop informants coming forward.

"We are entitled to disclosure of what happened between JPMorgan, the ACCC and ASIC in relation to these events," Mr Game said. They were "quite central" to the overall cartel case and raised questions about "the propriety of the ACCC".

But the magistrate agreed some parts of the documents could remain redacted. The case continues.

Key pointsANZ has questioned the ACCC's cartel investigation.

It claims the ACCC may have pressured ASIC to go easy on JPMorgan, its star witness.

HEADLINE: China lender sends receivers to Sargon
TEXT:
A Chinese lender has dispatched receivers to three companieslinked to the high-powered trustee and superannuation services outfit Sargon Capital.

The receivership came after Sargon Capital, whose board included big players such as former Crown Resorts chairman Robert Rankin and ALP Senator Stephen Conroy, struggled to raise funds in the past year.

The appointment of receivers Jason Preston and Shaun Fraser of McGrathNicol was executed this week. The other two companies are related to investment and advisory firm Trimantium, where 34 year old fintech entrepreneur Phillip Kingston is also chairman.

Sources with knowledge of the situation said the entities in receivership were not operating companies.

Trimantium did not respond to queries but Sargon Capital confirmed receivers were appointed by Chinese state-owned finance company Taiping Trustees, part of China Taiping Insurance Group.

Regulatory filings obtained by the Financial Review show China Taiping entities was the only security holder over the three entities, linked to three promissory notes from 2018 worth up to $HK500 million ($95.6 million) each and a loan in 2019 of up to $HK653 million ($124.9 million). The notes were all marked "Sargon".

Sources said Mr Rankin had resigned as chairman of Sargon Capital in January, with the move not related to the receivership. He is still listed in regulatory searches as a director and Mr Kingston as chief executive.

Melbourne-based Sargon Capital boasts it provides "trustee cloud infrastructure to power the world's next generation of funds and financial products", with over $55 billion in assets under trusteeship and supervision.

The company had looked a $1 billion-plus float on the sharemarket last year but this failed to come to fruition, while a further attempt at another equity raising also fizzled, according to the Financial Review's Street Talk column. The company had adopted a roll-up strategy, acquiring multiple financial service providers in recent years.

Jan Kolbusz, the founder of the Decimal digital financial advice software company acquired by Sargon in September 2018, said he was hopeful that the Decimal subsidiary - which is understood to be used by major superannuation players including QSuper and Mercer - would not be doomed by the development.

"There is no question about the quality of the technology there. It would be an absolute shame if the technology was lost to the industry because of this," he said. "The Hayne royal commission was very important but it also set back the market because it has distracted super funds and financial advisers. They can't look at implementing innovation at the moment."

Mr Kingston started the company in 2015 with Aron D'Souza.

Both men were reportedly linked to Silicon Valley titan Peter Thiel. Mr Thiel provided funds to Trimantium to acquire a small Adelaide wealth manager called Tidswell that was in possession of a licence to manage superannuation funds, but Mr Thiel later withdrew the investment.

It later emerged Mr D'Souza was the Mr 'A' mastermind behind Mr Thiel's plan to back wrestler Hulk Hogan's litigation of gossip website Gawker.

Hong Kong-based Trimantium boasted of an investment portfolio that included Sargon. The two Trimantium entities in receivership are Trimantium Capital Funds Management, which the company's website describes as a "trustee and investment manager of various wholesale investment products", and Trimantium Investment Management, which is fully owned by Trimantium Ltd. Both entities' sole director is Mr Kingston.

HEADLINE: NBN gives in to retailers in enterprise war
TEXT:
NBN Co says it will stop cutting deals directly with enterprise customers, in a surprise surrender to groups such as Telstra and Vocus that will end months of fighting.

The sudden submission will have NBN Co play a diminished role in the enterprise broadband market, acting exclusively through retail service providers (RSPs).

Business customers who want the NBN built to their premises will no longer be able to write contracts with NBN Co directly but must go through RSPs such as Telstra, Optus, Vocus, TPG or Macquarie Telecom.

Two days ago, NBN Co had made another big concession to retailers, signalling its intention to stop "over-building" fibre to business premises already served by private sector fibre.

Put together, these two concessions look like a total capitulation to the retailers' demands and should ease increasingly strained relations between the government-backed NBN and the private sector. NBN Co will continue to serve business customers, but only through RSPs.

"In response to this feedback, NBN Co will evolve its enterprise contracting model so that RSPs will in all cases have the direct contractual relationship with enterprise customers," NBN Co said in a statement yesterday.

"Previously, NBN Co has at times contracted directly with enterprise customers to build connectivity ahead of those customers engaging one or more RSPs to provide operational broadband services."

Paul Tyler, head of NBN Co's enterprise business, said the sudden decision came "partially in response to the level of noise that was building in the industry".

"It wasn't just from Telstra. We were getting consistent feedback from all players in the industry, and that changed over the last couple of weeks.

"To be successful in the long term, we need a constructive relationship with retailers. We need to have a vibrant diverse group of retailers who want to sell NBN products," he said.

But he said the U-turn would have no implications on the revenue of the enterprise business, which is projected to reach $1 billion a year by 2022.

Telstra immediately welcomed the decision, saying it was "pleased to see NBN Co has acknowledged the industry's view that it should not be contracting directly with customers".

"As we have said before, we believe that NBN contracting directly with end customers is not consistent with the legislation that governs the industry, and it needs to stop it now," a spokesman for the $46 billion telco giant said.

"NBN Co was established to be a wholesale-only provider and this is mandated in legislation. This was to ensure NBN did not engage in retail sales activities or preference itself or an RSP on pricing or terms of supply. The ACCC action last year revealed this was in fact happening."

Vocus chief executive Kevin Russell also welcomed both concessions, saying it had "been a very good couple of days for the industry".

"We had two fundamental concerns, and both of those have been addressed. We are really positive on the announcements this week. Really positive. Our focus is on how we can partner [with the NBN] to provide a better service in the market place," he said.

With NBN Co no longer cutting deals directly with businesses, RSPs that own fibre networks, such as Vocus, Telstra, Optus and TPG, will have a freer run at marketing their own fibre networks to business customers.

NBN Co is forbidden to act as a broadband retailer to either residential or business customers, but customers can directly contract NBN Co to build fibre to their premises.

NBN Co had been aggressively promoting this service directly to businesses and had already signed direct fibre-building contracts with the likes of Westpac and Australian Post.

This aggressive strategy enraged private-sector competitors, who complained that the government-owned broadband provider was breaching its strict remit as a wholesale-only provider. Mr Russell and Telstra chairman John Mullen had been the most outspoken critics.

NBN Co initially remained defiant. As recently as last week, NBN Co defended its right to sign building contracts with end-users and to overbuild fibre to premises already served by private sector fibre.

NBN Co said yesterday the federal government had no hand in the decision, which Communications Minister Paul Fletcher confirmed.

"Operational decisions, such as modifying the company's approach to the business segment, are commercial matters for NBN Co's board and management," Mr Fletcher said.

"NBN Co has decided to adjust its contracting model so that retailers will in all cases have the direct contractual relationship with enterprise customers. I am pleased that NBN Co is continuing to be responsive to industry feedback."

HEADLINE: How to revive your career post-Hayne
TEXT:
One year after the Hayne royal commission put Australia's financial services executives through the wringer, one thing is abundantly clear: if you didn't fare well, your best chance at rehabilitation was to fall on your sword and do it quickly.

As the year-long inquiry tore through the ranks of our top executives, AMP, NAB and IOOF would each lose their chairman, chief executive and at least two group executives.

Only a handful of those who faced off against Commissioner Hayne's counsel assisting over key issues have re-emerged in corporate life and many of those have moved great distances and been forced to accept slightly lower stations in life.

While NAB chief executive Andrew Thorburn and chairman Ken Henry chose to stick around for Commissioner Hayne's final denouement, group executive Andrew Hagger opted to leave before the writing was on the wall.

Mr Thorburn's status on a networking website is listed as "focused on actively exploring where I can make a positive impact for people", while Mr Henry retains his seat on the board of the ASX and some academic interests.

Mr Hagger had sparred with counsel assisting Michael Hodge over the fees-for-no-service issue, specifically the manner in which NAB informed the regulator about the extent of the problem and whether his intention was to manipulate its standing in a report.

An email conversation between Mr Hagger, Mr Thorburn and COO Antony Cahill was tendered in evidence. Although not implicated, Mr Cahill - viewed internally as a potential CEO - would up-sticks and move to Europe two weeks later taking up a post with VISA in London.

Mr Hagger would resign four weeks on, releasing a statement taking "accountability for what has occurred on my watch". He would pop up five months later as CEO of billionaire miner Andrew Forrest's charity and investment arm Minderoo.

The experience at AMP was not dissimilar. CEO Craig Meller was the first to leave after the firm's tricky dealings with ASIC over its fees-for-no-service problem were revealed.

Ten days later chairman Catherine Brenner and chief legal counsel Brian Salter followed suit. Ms Brenner only recently dipped her toe back into public life with a seat on the board of the George Institute for Global Health.

Later that year AMP's group executive of wealth and customer solutions, Paul Sainsbury, opted to retire after his appearance at the inquiry where he admitted it was company policy to charge dead customers life insurance premiums for up to three months.

Mr Sainsbury's LinkedIn profile lists his status as "On a break".

Of the four departures the only one to reappear in corporate life full-time is Brian Salter who has emerged as the interim executive manager of legal, governance and risk for Transgrid.

Commonwealth Bank did not face the same blitzkrieg as NAB or AMP but its group executives were equally battered. Head of Commonwealth Private Marianne Perkovic was forced to admit the bank's record keeping systems were hopeless, while executive general manager of Colonial First State Linda Elkins was told by counsel assisting the bank was a "gold medallist" for charging fees for no service.

Ms Perkovic, a former executive with Count Plus, had the good fortune of having some of her reflections read in the final session of hearings, where she apologised for letting the community down and not speaking up. She remains with the company. But Ms Elkins has opted to start afresh, taking the leadership role at KPMG's asset and wealth management team from former union figure Paul Howes.

Over at wealth manager IOOF the path to redemption has not been so easy. Grilled for a series of infractions related to its conflicted structure and propensity to dip into the members' reserves, the company lost its chairman and CEO in quick succession only for its chief financial officer and legal counsel to ultimately fall victim to a reshuffle late last year.

Former CEO Chris Kelaher's appearance at the royal commission was characterised by a sense of indifference, something the commissioner seized on during one of his rare interjections.

The final nail in the coffin for the chairman and executives came several months later when the prudential regulator sought to ban IOOF from the superannuation industry for not being "fit and proper". IOOF fought the action and was ultimately successful. But at the conclusion of a business review by new CEO Renato Mota, CFO David Coulter and chief legal counsel Gary Riordan found themselves extraneous to the company's needs in December.

News Corp's new CFO Michael Ford coming off QBE shocker

News Corp Australia has appointed its latest chief financial officer. Former QBE Insurance CFO Michael Ford assumes the ceremonial office being vacated by Stacey Brown in April.

Brown served in a purely decorative capacity inside the knotty refinancing of Foxtel last year led by News Corp's global CFO Susan Panuccio, Brown's predecessor at Holt Street.

Ford's investiture on Mahogany Row - between Panuccio's pin cushion Michael Miller and certifiable nincompoop Damian Eales - will be nothing if not entertaining.

He had been at QBE for an entire seven months when his resignation was curtly included in a broader announcement to the ASX. "I would like to ... thank Michael for his time at QBE," was all chief executive Pat Regan said. Effusive!

By no accident, Ford barely said a word during his only set of results in February 2018. Through the subsequent investor meetings, he maintained a monastic silence.

Sadly, his vow did not survive management's sit-down with sophisticated insurance investor, JCP Investment Partners. After Regan and QBE's Australia chief Vivek Bhatia had presented, one of JCP's portfolio managers insisted on an insurance terminology pop quiz for the mute, new numbers man. First up, Ford couldn't summon the meaning of IBNER (incurred but not enough reported) - a disturbing gotcha for his hosts given the centrality of aggressive reserving to QBE's run of earnings downgrades under John Neal.

The poor bloke then fluffed another couple of questions consecutively. At none from three, Regan mercifully stepped in and ended the humiliation.

Ford was previously deputy CFO at the CBA, and the incident does support the market gripe that bankers know little about the intricacies of insurance.

Never mind - Ford has now found himself the perfect workplace in the perfect industry. Across the hall, Eales can barely read the newspapers, let alone sell them.

What has happened to Rio Tinto?

It was a telling garnish on the whole sorry affair: three days into The Australian's exposure of Rio Tinto's Orwellian "dynamic discounting" program screwing its suppliers, the miner's chief commercial officer Simon Trott was, well, trotted out to front the grovelling backdown. Group chief executive Jean-Sébastien Jacques exhibited his kind of leadership from the distant rear. In no way is the man more French than in his truancy of character.

Rio's behaviour under Jacques gives rise to its increasing isolation.

Only in October, a House of Representatives standing committee held an inquiry "into how the mining sector can support businesses in regional economies" and received submissions from BHP, Glencore and the Minerals Council of Australia; but not a peep from Rio. The inquiry's first term of reference was "the appropriateness of the payment terms offered to businesses by the mining sector". Engaged in an AI-driven supply chain shakedown, what could Rio have possibly tendered?

Last month, the Takeovers Panel found adversely against Rio's attempt to underwrite an equity raising in Energy Resources of Australia to dilute the uranium miner's minority shareholders into oblivion. Rio's representative ERA director even attended meetings of its board's "independent panel" assessing the deal.

For its Bell Bay and Tomago aluminium smelters in Tasmania and New South Wales, Rio has been gouging cheaper (read: subsidised) electricity from those state governments and holding the futures of local workers over their heads. It's called extortion.

And Rio's indecent mania for greenwashing - claiming risible "fossil free" leadership while denying its Scope 3 emissions responsibility, which BHP and Vale have accepted - has been well-established.

What has happened to Rio Tinto's hallowed conduct manual, The Way We Work, alleged breaches of which were once enough to sack members of Jacques' group executive committee and are still deemed sufficient to withhold remuneration entitlements from Jacques' predecessor Sam Walsh?!

"In everything we do, we hold ourselves accountable to the highest industry standards and our own stringent requirements for ethical conduct," it pledges. Yet time and again over the past three years, Rio has been, demonstrably, a bad faith actor in Australian society.

And the miner's board of directors - sitting far, far away from any red dirt, twirling their mustaches atop St James's Square - has been utterly inanimate, rendered so by their plenteous profits.

Our eminent neighbour Chanticleer landed it impeccably yesterday: "It's as if [they] have learnt nothing from the way the banks' relentless focus on profits above all else brought them unstuck."

Or, in the words of Small Business Ombudsman Kate Carnell, "how ordinary is that?" Harvey flogs cucumber operation after manager's conviction

Alas, Gerry Harvey's presumed plans to dominate the global tzatziki trade have come to an end.

A year after selling his Coomboona dairy farm, he's now flogging his 5-hectare state-of-the-art artisanal cucumber operation at Peats Ridge.

Unlike Coomboona, a controversial and ultimately lousy investment by Harvey-controlled retailer Harvey Norman, Family Fresh Farms is (for now) owned directly by the billionaire. Who only last August was spruiking his "not-so-little secret passion project" where seasonal workers from Vanuatu pick millions of hydroponic baby cucumbers.

Harvey has been raising cash of late. He put up $120 million of his Harvey Norman shares as collateral for an ANZ personal loan in December. But in the case of Peats Ridge, in particular, we wonder if the jailing earlier this month of Family Fresh Farms' facility manager Andrew Young put a spanner in the works.

Young was a founding director of whitegoods appliance brand Kleenmaid, which collapsed in 2009 owing $96 million. Three weeks ago, he was found guilty of insolvent trading and of defrauding Westpac of $13 million by dishonestly gaining a loan. After a lengthy jury trial in Brisbane, Young was refused bail until his February sentencing hearing.

Young was charged all the way back in 2012. That is, well before he started working for Harvey. With whom he presumably had professional history, Kleenmaid appliances having been stocked by Harvey Norman before the former's collapse. Few would employ someone with a criminal charge hanging over their heads, but clearly, Harvey takes supplier relations more seriously than most.

The billionaire paid $5 million for the Peats Ridge site in May 2013 and didn't do much with it for several years. Local rumour holds his original intention had been to harvest a medicinal marijuana crop, but when the licensing didn't work out, he turned to cucumbers instead, spending $20 million building the current facility which opened in 2017.

Along the way, Harvey also coughed up $15,000 in fines to the New South Wales Environmental Protection Authority, after a site visit in May of that year uncovered it burning woodchips to heat its greenhouses before it had secured the necessary licences.
